Sample text:
---
I have never been able to keep a proper diary. The blank page makes me perform, so I write instead on backs of envelopes, in the margins of library books I technically should not be writing in, on the fogged bathroom mirror after a shower, and in a small black notebook that lives in the left pocket of my coat. It is not a record of my life. It is a collection of evidence that I was paying attention.

That, I think, is enough. Attention is a much more forgiving project than memory. Memory insists on sequence and significance and a tidy arc from first page to last. Attention only asks that you notice the way the bus driver taps his fingers against the steering wheel when he is waiting for the light, or the exact shade of green that appears on the underside of a leaf when you flip it over in August. It asks nothing more heroic than that.

The old word for such a notebook was commonplace book, which sounds dull now, like a place where common things are kept, but in the seventeenth century it was a serious intellectual practice. Students copied out quotations they admired, summarized arguments, pasted in receipts for ink, drew little diagrams of arguments as branching trees. It was less about originality than about digestion. You read something, you chewed it until it was part of you, and then you wrote it down in your own hand so your hand would remember it later.

I walk the same route most mornings, not because I am disciplined or because I have read somewhere that walking is good for the soul, although both of those things are probably true, but because the route has taught me things a new route cannot. I know which corner floods when it rains hard, which dog barks at the mailman and which one only pretends to, where the lilacs overhang the fence in May and where the sidewalk is cracked in a way that always catches my heel if I am not looking down. Repetition is a kind of intimacy.

Forgetting is usually treated as a failure, a leak in the system. But I have come to think of it as an editor. It removes the sentences that were only there to fill space. I do not remember most conversations I have had, and that is a mercy. I remember the way a friend laughed when she was nervous in a job interview and told me about it later, losing the thread of her own story and laughing again. I remember that the cat we had when I was twelve used to sleep with his head inside my empty shoe, but I cannot remember the color of the walls in that house. The editor decided.

I love secondhand bookshops for the same reason I love old notebooks: they are full of other people's attention. Someone has underlined a sentence in a novel about guilt, or written in pencil on the flyleaf, 'return to p. 47, this is important,' and never came back. I find those notes more moving than any dedication. A dedication is public. A marginal note is private and practical. It says: I was here, I was confused or moved, and I wanted to leave a breadcrumb for a future self who might be smarter or sadder or simply less hurried.

My kitchen is not a good kitchen. The burners are uneven, the drawer for knives sticks in humid weather, and the window above the sink has never quite closed properly since I moved in. But it is where I think best, perhaps because I have to stand still in one place while water boils. The kettle is a very old-fashioned one that whistles instead of clicking off. While I wait, I find myself rehearsing conversations, apologizing to people in my head for small offenses that probably did not register, deciding what to do with the rest of the day. Tea gives me an excuse to pause without calling it a pause.

I have always wanted to be the kind of person who could read a map the way other people read a letter, easily and without embarrassment. I am not. I turn the map around, I orient myself by shop signs, I ask strangers for directions with a confidence I do not feel. And yet I collect maps, old ones especially, with their careful hatching for forests that no longer exist and their confident labels for villages that have changed names twice since the map was printed. A map is a guess made beautiful. It says: this is how the world looked from a height, at a moment, to someone who needed to get somewhere else.

Words lose their meaning if I say them too often. Try it with 'door' or 'window' or 'table.' Say it twenty times and it becomes a sound, a piece of nonsense, a small animal that has escaped its cage. That is why I distrust people who use the same big words for everything important. If every sorrow is tragic and every joy is transcendent, then nothing is. I prefer the small, precise words we use in kitchens and workshops and on walks: damp, propped, rattling, late, nearly, enough. They have not been worn smooth by overuse.

And so I keep going, not toward any great revelation but toward the next ordinary hour, which is where revelations usually hide if they hide at all. I will write another sentence in the notebook, take another walk past the lilacs, wait for the kettle, and forget, gratefully, most of what I said today. If you ask me what I have learned, I will probably say something imprecise and then correct myself, which is another way of paying attention. The light will turn the color of weak tea again, and I will be there to notice it, and that, for now, seems enough. And that, I think, is where I will leave it.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A first-person reflective essay turns small habits and observations into a quietly lyrical account of paying attention.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, measured, and gently self-correcting: it admits imperfect habits and uncertainties without making them into grand confessions. Its pathos lies in the wish to keep traces of a life while accepting that memory edits and forgets; notebooks, marginal notes, familiar routes, and pauses over tea become modest forms of connection. The invitation is to notice the ordinary with care, and to let “enough” be enough.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds attention over memory, repetition as intimacy, and private traces left in notebooks and secondhand books. It finds meaning in ordinary objects and acts—the kettle, a map, a leaf, a familiar walk—and favors precise everyday words over inflated claims. Its closing mood is grateful and unhurried rather than revelatory.

## Evidence line
> Repetition is a kind of intimacy.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive, coherent preoccupation with attention through recurring objects and images, rather than relying on a generic thesis alone.
